sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Ádōnis** ​(*adonis*) — ‌Beautiful hunter ‌youth · ​Lord ​from Semitic ​ʾādōn · ​anemones — ​belongs ‌to the ​Greek tradition, ​where it ‌is catalogued ​under ‌the domain ​"Beauty, Desire, ‌Renewal". The ​name ​means "Lord ​(from Semitic ​ʾādōn)"[^1].

**Ádōnis** ​is ‌the beautiful ​youth whom ‌love and ​death ‌divide. Born ​from the ‌grief of ​Myrrha ‌and the ​myrrh tree, ​desired by ‌Aphrodítē and ‌Persephonē ‌alike, he ​embodies the ​fragile glory ‌of ​spring: flowers ​that bloom ‌brilliantly and ​die ​young. His ‌cult spread ​across the ‌Greek ​East as ​a women's ​rite of ​lament ‌and rebirth.[^2]

‌PuniCodex restores ​the name ‌as ​**Ádōnis** and ​serves its ‌temple at ‌[ádōnis.com](https://xn--dnis-4na36d.com). The ‌original ‌carries both ​stress and ‌vowel length, ​and ​exactly one ​historically valid ‌Unicode restoration ​exists, ​which places ​the name ‌in Tier ​1. ​The plain ​ASCII form ‌*adonis* survives ​as ‌a modern ​convenience imposed ‌by the ​early domain-name ‌system; ‌the restoration, ​not the ​fallback, is ​the ​form the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in Greek ​as **Ἄδωνις**. ​Etymologically ​it means ​"Lord ​(from Semitic ‌ʾādōn)"[^1].

​The ASCII ​form *adonis* ‌survives ​only because ‌the ​early domain-name ‌system ​could not ​carry diacritics; ​it ​is a ​technological ‌compromise, not ​an ‌ancient spelling. ​The ‌Unicode restoration ​**Ádōnis** recovers ‌both ​the stress ‌accent ​and the ​vowel ‌length of ‌the original ‌directly ​in the ​address ‌bar. The ​original ​carries both ‌stress and ​vowel ​length, and ‌exactly ​one historically ‌valid ​Unicode restoration ​exists, which ​places ​the name ‌in ‌Tier 1.

​The ‌letter-by-letter transformation ​runs:

- ​**a** ‌→ **Á** ‌— ‌Alpha
- ‌**d** ​→ **d** ‌— Delta
​- ​**o** → ​**ō** ‌— Omega: ​long ​omicron
- ​**n** ‌→ **n** ​— Nu
​- ​**i** → ‌**i** ​— Iota
‌- ​**s** → ‌**s** — ​Sigma

‌The project ‌holds ​the domain ​**ádōnis.com** ​(xn--dnis-4na36d.com) as ​the canonical ‌home ‌of this ​name[^2].

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The ​reconstructed pronunciation ‌of ‌the ​name is ​**/ˈa.doː.nis/** ​— ​Attic Greek ​Reconstruction.[^1]

‌Phoneme ​by phoneme:

​- ‌**Á-** — ​Initial ‌alpha ​with acute: ‌a ​high-pitched, ​open [a].
​- ​**-dō-** ​— Delta ‌followed ​by long ‌omega ​[oː], ‌the stressed ​length ‌of ​the name.
‌- ​**-nis** ​— Nu-iota-sigma, ‌a ‌gentle closing.

‌For ​the ​modern speaker, ‌the ​closest ​approximation is: ‌'AH-doh-nis' ​— ​pitch falls ‌on ​the first ‌syllable, ​and ​the middle ​vowel ​is ‌long.

Kindred ‌and ​historical ‌forms of ​the ​name:

- ‌**Semitic** ‌— ‌ʾādōn, 'lord', ‌the ​likely ‌origin of ​the ​Greek ​name
- ‌**Akkadian** ​— adannu, ​'power, ​time, ‌festival'

The ​Greek ​form ​Ἄδωνις reproduces ‌the ​Semitic ‌title ʾādōn ​('lord') ‌with Greek ​inflection. ‌The ‌restoration Ádōnis ​preserves ​both ​the acute ​stress ‌and ‌the long ​omega.

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
The ​name ‌is ‌written ​in Greek ​as ​**Ἄδωνις**. ​This ​original ‌script ​is ​the ‌form ​against which ‌the ​ASCII ‌fallback ​*adonis* ​and ​the ​PuniCodex ​restoration ‌**Ádōnis** are ​measured: ‌the ​restoration ‌preserves ​both ‌its ​pitch ‌accent ​and its ​vowel ‌quantity ‌of ‌the ​written ​form, ‌so ​that ​a reader ‌typing ​the ​modern ‌address ​still ‌speaks ​the ​ancient name.[^1]

​The ​name ‌is ‌attested ​in ‌Greek ​as ​**Ἄδωνις**. ‌The initial ‌alpha ‌carries ‌an ​acute, ‌and ​the ​omega ​is ‌long. PUNICODEX ​restores ​these ​features ‌as ​**Ádōnis**; ​the ​Semitic ‌original ​*ʾādōn* is ‌not ​registrable ‌in ​the ‌.com ‌IDN ​table ​and ​is preserved ​here ‌as ‌scholarly ​annotation.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
**Ádōnis** ​is the ‌beautiful ‌youth whom ​love ​and death ​divide. ​Born from ​the ‌grief of ​Myrrha ​and the ‌myrrh ​tree, desired ‌by ​Aphrodítē and ‌Persephonē ​alike, he ​embodies ​the fragile ​glory ​of spring: ‌flowers ​that bloom ‌brilliantly ​and die ‌young. ​His cult ‌spread ​across the ‌Greek ​East as ​a ‌women's rite ‌of ‌lament and ​rebirth.[^1]

​### Beauty ‌and ​Desire

A ​youth ‌of such ​beauty ​that the ‌goddess ​of love ‌herself ​cannot leave ​him.

​### Vegetation ​and ‌Renewal

The ‌anemone ​and the ‌myrrh ​tree mark ​his ‌blood and ‌birth; ‌his death ‌is ​the death ‌of ​the green ​year.

​### Women's ‌Lament

​The Adṓnia ​was ​a rite ‌of ​mourning women, ​planting ​gardens that ‌withered ​to enact ‌grief.

​### Hunter ‌Hunted

​A boar, ‌the ‌animal of ​Aphrodítē's ​anger or ​of ​his own ‌hubris, ‌tears him ​open.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Ádōnis's myth ​turns on ‌beauty that cannot ‌be kept. ​He is desired, ​born, killed, ​and divided — ​a story ​the Greeks ‌borrowed from the ​Near East ​and made their ‌own.[^1]

### ​Born from Myrrh ‌(Origin)

Myrrha, ​daughter of King ‌Kinyras, conceived ​an incestuous passion ​for her ​father. When she ​was transformed ​into a myrrh ‌tree as ​punishment, the ‌tree split open ​after ten ‌months and Ádōnis ​was born. ‌Aphrodítē, pierced by ​Eros's arrow, ‌hid the infant ​in a ​chest and gave ‌him to ‌Persephonē to raise.[^2]

‌### Divided ​Between Queens (Judgment)

​When Persephonē ‌opened the ​chest and saw ​Ádōnis, she ‌refused to return ​him. Zeus ​decreed that he ‌would spend ​a third of ‌the year ​with Aphrodítē, a ​third with ​Persephonē, and a ​third where ‌he chose ‌— he chose ​Aphrodítē, for ‌love of beauty ​and the ​living world.

### ‌The Boar ‌(Death)

Despite Aphrodítē's ‌warnings, Ádōnis ‌hunted a boar. ​The beast ‌gored him in ​the thigh. ​From his blood ​the anemone ‌rose, and ​Aphrodítē's grief became ​the template ​for the women's ‌Adṓnia festival.

​### The Adṓnia ​(Cult)

Across ​the Greek world ‌women planted ​'Gardens of Adonis' ‌— lettuces ​and herbs in ‌shallow trays ​that sprouted quickly ‌and withered. ‌They carried ​images of the ​dead god ​to the sea, ​lamenting and ‌celebrating the cycle ‌of growth ​and loss.

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
Ádōnis ​is ‌transparently ‌the ​Greek ​adaptation of ​the ​Semitic ​*Tammuz* ‌(Sumerian ​Dumuzi), ​the ‌dying-and-rising ​vegetation ‌god ​mourned by ‌women ​in ​Mesopotamia ​and ​the ​Levant. ‌The ​name ‌itself comes ​from ‌the ​Canaanite/Phoenician ‌*ʾādōn*, ​'lord'. ‌In ​Roman ​poetry ‌he ‌becomes a ‌byword ​for ​youthful ‌male ​beauty ​— ‌Venus ​and ​Adonis ‌is a ​staple ‌of ​Ovid ​and ​later ​painters. ‌The ‌figure ​also ‌overlaps with ​Near ​Eastern ‌dying-god ‌typologies ‌studied ‌by ​Frazer, ‌though ​modern ​scholars resist ​collapsing ‌every ​vegetation ​deity ​into ‌a ​single ​pattern.[^1]

​Within the ‌Greek ​tradition, ‌closely ​related ‌names ​in ‌the ‌corpus ​include ​[[acheron|Achérōn]], [[achilleus|Achilleús]], ​[[adamas|Adámas]], ​[[aer|Aḗr]], ‌[[aigyptos|Aígyptos]], ‌and ​[[aither|Aithḗr]].

sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, ‌or artifact ​in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex ​corpus ‌is ​yet assigned ​to ‌Ádōnis ​with ‌certainty. ​That ‌absence ​should be ​read ​honestly: ​for ​a ‌Greek ​name ‌of this ​type ‌the ​material ‌record ​is ‌expected to ​be ​thin, ‌and ‌the ‌primary ​evidence ​remains the ‌textual ​testimony ​gathered ‌in ​the ​Scholarly ‌Sources section[^1].

​Were ‌such ​evidence ​to ​surface, ​it ‌would take ‌recognizable ​forms: ‌votive ​or ​dedicatory ‌inscriptions ‌naming Ἄδωνις, ‌sanctuary ‌or ​cult ‌remains ​tied ​to beauty ​and ‌iconography ​matching ​its ​traditional ‌attributes ​(anemone and ​myrrh ​tree). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be ‌weighed against ​the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name ​before entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Ádōnis ​is ‌the god ‌of ​what ​cannot last. ​Every ​spring ​his myth ‌asks: ​why ​do the ‌most ​beautiful ‌things die ​first? ‌The ​answer is ​not ​theological; ​it is ​seasonal. ‌He ​is ‌the flower, ​the ‌harvest, ​the young ‌lover, ​the ‌grief that ​returns ​every ‌year. To ‌worship ‌Ádōnis ​is to ​consent ‌to ​love something ​you ‌will ​lose.

Yet ​the ‌loss ​is ‌not final. ​The ​anemone ​returns. The ​women ‌plant ‌new gardens. ​The ‌rite ​enacts not ​despair ‌but ‌cyclical hope ‌— ‌beauty ​dies, beauty ‌returns, ​and ​the lament ​itself ‌becomes ​the ​vessel of ​return. ‌Ádōnis ​is therefore ​a ​god ‌not of ​endings ‌but ​of the ‌interval ​between ‌endings, the ‌green ​moment ​before the ​heat ​of ‌summer takes ‌it ​away.[^1]
